title: Entity–Relationship (ER) Modelling
tagline: Draw the business before you write a single CREATE TABLE.
explain: An ER model is a drawing of your data before you build any tables: which things you store (entities), what you know about each (attributes), and how they connect (relationships). You do it first because changing a table layout after millions of rows exist is slow and risky, while changing a drawing is free.
## The three building blocks

- Entity: a thing you keep records about, such as Customer, Order, Product. It becomes a table.
- Attribute: a fact about an entity, such as an order's created_at or a product's price. It becomes a column.
- Relationship: how two entities relate, such as a customer places orders. It becomes a foreign key, or a separate table.
Try it: click each part to see what it turns into.
@viz:er-anatomy
## Cardinality: how many on each side
Ask two questions for every pair of entities. 'How many B can one A have?' and 'How many A can one B have?' The answers give the type of relationship, and the type decides the table layout.

- One-to-many (1:N): one customer has many orders, each order has one customer. Put the foreign key on the many side: orders.customer_id. This is the most common case by far.
- Many-to-many (M:N): a student takes many courses and a course has many students. A column cannot hold this cleanly, so you add a junction (join) table with two foreign keys: enrollment(student_id, course_id).
- One-to-one (1:1): a user has one profile. Put a unique foreign key on one side. Use it to split rarely used or sensitive columns out of a hot table.
On a real ER diagram these counts are drawn as symbols at the ends of the line (crow's-foot notation). Pick a symbol for each end and read the sentence it makes.
@viz:er-notation

> Shop. A customer places many orders (1:N). An order contains many products and a product appears in many orders (M:N), so you need order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price). Notice that quantity and unit_price describe the pairing, not the order or the product alone. Any fact about the relationship itself lives in the junction table.
A common slip is putting the foreign key on the wrong table. Test yourself:
@viz:fk-side
## Rules that keep the model honest

- Every table gets a primary key that never changes. Prefer a surrogate id over a natural value such as email, because natural values change.
- Store a fact in exactly one place. If you copy it elsewhere, you must keep both copies in sync by hand (see Normalization).
- Decide optional vs required up front. A nullable column means 'this fact may be unknown', and every query touching it must handle NULL.
- Name things for the business, not for the screen. A table called Order survives a redesign. A table called CheckoutPageData does not.
## Putting it together: design a schema
Here is the whole process on one small example. Step through it and notice where each rule above is used.
@viz:er-design
## From drawing to Django

In Django each entity is a Model class, ForeignKey is the 1:N link, ManyToManyField creates the junction table for you, and OneToOneField is the 1:1 link. When the junction table carries its own facts (quantity, price), declare it yourself and pass it with through=, as in the code below.

The question interviewers ask is almost always the same: here is a product (a ride-hailing app, a library, an e-commerce site), design the tables. Walk them through your steps: list entities, list relationships with cardinality, name the keys, then say where you would add indexes and what you would store redundantly for speed and why.
keyPoints: Entities → tables, attributes → columns, relationships → FKs / junction tables.
1–1, 1–N, N–M. N–M is always resolved with a junction table.
Mark optionality (nullable FK) and uniqueness rules on the diagram.
The ERD is a living document: commit it next to the schema.

interview.q: How do you model a many-to-many relationship?
interview.a: With a junction table holding two FKs, ideally with a composite PK (or a surrogate PK + UNIQUE on the pair). If the relationship has attributes (quantity, sort_order), it becomes a first-class entity — in Django, a through model.

interview.q: How would you model one-to-one in SQL?
interview.a: A FK on the dependent table that is also UNIQUE (or is the PK). Django: OneToOneField.

basis: Mid priority. Schema design is a mid-level expectation.

title: Primary and Foreign Keys
tagline: Identity and referential integrity — the spine of every schema.
explain: A key is how the database identifies a row, and a foreign key is how one table safely points to another. Almost every bug involving 'orphan data' or 'duplicate users' is a key that was missing or wrong.
## The kinds of key

- Candidate key: any column or set of columns that is unique and never NULL for every row. A table can have several candidates.
- Primary key (PK): the one candidate you choose as the official identity. Exactly one per table, never NULL, never reused. It is automatically indexed.
- Unique key: a column that must be unique but is not the PK, such as email. It may allow NULL.
- Foreign key (FK): a column whose value must exist as a key in another table. It is the database enforcing 'this order belongs to a real customer'.
- Composite key: a key made of more than one column, common in junction tables, such as (student_id, course_id).
## Surrogate vs natural keys

A natural key is a real-world value such as email or passport number. A surrogate key is an id invented by the database (an auto-increment integer or a UUID) that means nothing outside the table. Surrogate keys are the default choice because real-world values change (people change email, countries change codes), and when a PK changes every foreign key pointing to it must change too. Keep natural values as UNIQUE columns instead.

- Auto-increment integer: small, fast, ordered inserts, easy to read. Downside: guessable (/orders/101 invites /orders/102) and awkward to generate across several databases.
- UUID: can be generated anywhere without coordination, hard to guess. Downside: 16 bytes, and random UUIDs scatter inserts across the index, which slows writes on very large tables. Time-ordered UUIDs reduce that cost.
## What a foreign key actually does

A foreign key makes the database reject two kinds of mistakes. You cannot insert an order for a customer that does not exist. And you cannot delete a customer who still has orders, unless you chose a rule for what happens. That rule is the ON DELETE action:

- RESTRICT or NO ACTION: refuse the delete. Safest default for important data.
- CASCADE: delete the child rows too. Right for data that has no meaning alone, such as order lines when an order is deleted. Dangerous for anything you want to keep.
- SET NULL: keep the child and blank the link. The FK column must allow NULL.

> You delete user 7. With CASCADE every order of user 7 disappears, and with it your revenue history. With RESTRICT the delete fails and forces you to decide. This is why Django's on_delete argument is mandatory: the framework makes you choose.
## Following keys: joins
The reason foreign keys exist is that you can follow them. A JOIN combines rows from two tables where the key values match. The join type decides what happens to rows that find no match.
@viz:joins
## Indexing and foreign keys

A primary key gets an index automatically. A foreign key in PostgreSQL does not. Joins and deletes on the parent table search the child by FK, so an unindexed FK on a big table turns a parent delete into a full scan of the child. Django adds an index to ForeignKey columns for you, but if you design tables by hand, add it.
Interview angle: expect 'PK vs unique key', 'why surrogate keys', 'what does ON DELETE CASCADE do and when is it dangerous', and 'is a foreign key indexed automatically'.
keyPoints: PK = UNIQUE + NOT NULL, one per table; implemented with a unique index.
FK enforces integrity; PostgreSQL does NOT auto-index the referencing column — add one.
Natural vs surrogate: business values change, surrogate IDs do not.
ON DELETE is a business decision, not a default.

django.title: ForeignKey, on_delete and db_index
django.code:
class Order(models.Model):
    customer = models.ForeignKey(
        "Customer",
        on_delete=models.PROTECT,      # RESTRICT: can't delete a customer who has orders
        related_name="orders",
    )
    # Django DOES create an index for ForeignKey by default (db_index=True),
    # unlike raw PostgreSQL.
django.note: Django emulates on_delete in Python (the ORM collects and deletes related rows itself); the FK constraint it creates in PostgreSQL has no ON DELETE action. Raw SQL deletes therefore bypass CASCADE. Worth mentioning in interviews.

exercise: Create product_categories with a composite primary key. Insert a row that references a missing product and read the error message carefully.
pitfalls: Using email as a PK, then needing to change an email.
Not indexing FK columns → slow joins and slow parent deletes (the DB must scan the child table).
Blanket ON DELETE CASCADE that silently wipes financial history.

interview.q: Difference between a primary key and a unique constraint?
interview.a: Both enforce uniqueness. A PK is the table’s chosen row identifier and is NOT NULL; a table has one PK but may have many UNIQUE constraints (which allow NULLs). PostgreSQL implements both with unique indexes.

interview.q: When would you use a composite key?
interview.a: For identity that is naturally a pair, e.g. (order_id, product_id) in order_items. Alternative: surrogate PK + UNIQUE(order_id, product_id) — easier to reference from other tables and friendlier to ORMs (Django has no composite PK for years; 5.2 added CompositePrimaryKey).

interview.q: Does PostgreSQL index a foreign key column automatically?
interview.a: No — it indexes the referenced PK/unique side only. Index the referencing column yourself (Django does by default).

basis: Core. Keys, indexes and SQL injection are named as the junior database bar.

title: Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF)
tagline: Every fact stored once, in the table it belongs to.
explain: Normalization is the discipline of storing each fact in exactly one place. It exists to prevent three bugs, called anomalies, that appear when the same fact is copied into many rows.
## The three anomalies

> A single table orders(order_id, customer_name, customer_city, product, price) repeats the customer's name and city on every order.
Update anomaly: the customer moves, you update 3 of their 5 rows and the other 2 now disagree.
Insert anomaly: you cannot record a new customer until they place an order.
Delete anomaly: delete their only order and you also lose the customer's details.
## The normal forms, in plain language
Each form is a stricter rule. A table in 3NF is also in 2NF and 1NF. For work and for interviews, 3NF is the target.

- 1NF: each cell holds one value, and there are no repeating groups. A column phones = '555-1, 555-2' breaks it. Fix: one row per phone in a separate table.
- 2NF: applies when the key has more than one column. Every non-key column must depend on the whole key, not just part of it. In order_items(order_id, product_id, product_name, qty), product_name depends only on product_id, so it belongs in products.
- 3NF: non-key columns must depend on the key and nothing else. In employees(id, dept_id, dept_name), dept_name depends on dept_id, not on the employee, so it belongs in departments.
- BCNF: a slightly stricter 3NF. Mention it if asked, but 3NF is almost always enough.
- 4NF: a table must not hold two independent lists about the same thing. If an employee has skills and languages that have nothing to do with each other, storing them together forces every skill to be paired with every language (2 skills x 2 languages = 4 rows, and adding one skill means adding a row per language). Fix: employee_skills and employee_languages.
- 5NF: if a table can be split into smaller tables and joined back to give exactly the same rows, split it. It matters for three-way relationships such as rep, company and product, where the rows are fully determined by three pairwise facts. It is only valid when that business rule is really true.
A memory line interviewers like: every non-key attribute must depend on 'the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key'.

How far to go: 1NF to 3NF are the working standard and what interviews expect. BCNF is usually reached with 3NF. 4NF and 5NF are rare. Know what they mean and when to look for them (independent lists in one table, or a three-way relationship), but you will seldom design for them. Open the animation and use the second tab to see each form break and then get fixed.
## How to normalize a table, step by step

- Write down the key and list every column.
- For each column ask: which key part determines this value? If only part of it, move it out (2NF).
- For each column ask: does this value actually depend on another non-key column? If so, move that pair out (3NF).
- Replace the moved-out columns with a foreign key to the new table.
Watch one flat table get split, one rule at a time:
@viz:decompose
## The cost of normalizing

Normalized data needs joins to put the picture back together. That is cheap when columns are indexed and tables are moderate, and costly when a hot query joins six huge tables. That trade-off is the entire reason Denormalization exists. The rule used in practice: normalize first, measure, then denormalize deliberately where a measured query needs it.

In Django this is simply: one model per fact, and ForeignKey instead of copied CharFields. If you catch yourself writing customer_name on an Order model, ask whether it should be a ForeignKey to Customer.
keyPoints: 1NF atomic · 2NF no partial dependency · 3NF no transitive dependency.
Normalize to remove update / insert / delete anomalies.
Normalize by default, denormalize with measured evidence.
"Why does this table exist?" should have a one-sentence answer.

sql.code:
-- Bad: one flat sheet
-- order_id | customer_name | customer_city | product_1 | product_2

-- Better
customers(id, name, email)
addresses(id, customer_id → customers, city, ...)
orders(id, customer_id → customers, created_at)
products(id, sku, name, price)
order_items(order_id → orders, product_id → products, quantity, unit_price)

django.title: Normalized models, no repeated groups
django.code:
class OrderItem(models.Model):
    order = models.ForeignKey(Order, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="items")
    product = models.ForeignKey(Product, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    quantity = models.PositiveIntegerField()
    unit_price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=12, decimal_places=2)  # deliberate snapshot

exercise: Normalize a flat sales table step by step (1NF → 2NF → 3NF). For each decomposition, explain which insert/update/delete anomaly disappeared.
pitfalls: Believing normalization is "always better" — it is a starting point.
Stopping at 1NF and leaving transitive dependencies (zip → city).
Confusing the need for a snapshot (unit_price) with a normalization violation.

interview.q: Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF with an example.
interview.a: Take orders(order_id, product_id, product_name, customer_name, customer_city). Atomic cells = 1NF. product_name depends only on product_id (part of key) → partial dependency, move to products (2NF). customer_city depends on customer_name, not on the key → transitive, move to customers (3NF).

interview.q: What anomalies does normalization prevent?
interview.a: Update (inconsistent copies), insert (cannot store a fact without an unrelated one) and delete (losing a fact when deleting an unrelated one).

basis: Core. Normalization/design is a recurring SQL-round topic.

title: Denormalization
tagline: Duplicate on purpose, and pay the consistency bill knowingly.
explain: Denormalization means deliberately storing a fact in more than one place to make reads faster or simpler. It is a trade, not a mistake: you pay in write complexity and risk of inconsistency, and you get faster reads. Do it only after normalizing and measuring.
## When it is the right move

- A hot read query joins many tables and shows up in your slow query log, and indexes alone did not fix it.
- The data is rarely updated but often read, such as a product's category name on a listing page.
- You need history: an invoice must keep the price the customer paid, even if the product price changes later.
- Reporting or search needs flat, pre-computed rows.
## Common techniques

- Copy a column: store customer_name on the order. Fast to read, but you must decide what happens when the source changes.
- Snapshot a value: store unit_price on the order line at purchase time. This is not a duplicate you must sync. It is a historical fact, and it is the one denormalization that is nearly always correct.
- Derived counters: store comment_count on a post so lists do not run COUNT(*) for every row. Update it in the same transaction as the comment insert.
- Summary tables and materialized views: pre-computed aggregates, refreshed on a schedule or by trigger.
- Caching in Redis is a form of denormalization with an expiry, covered under Consistency.
## The price you pay
Every copy needs an owner and an update rule. If you duplicate a value and never say who keeps it correct, you get the update anomaly from Normalization. Typical safeguards:

- Update both copies in one transaction.
- Use a database trigger or a Django signal, accepting that signals can be skipped by bulk operations.
- Rebuild the copy from the source on a schedule, and accept that it can be stale for a short time.
- Add a check job that compares the two and reports drift.

> A post list shows 'comments: 42'. Option A: COUNT(*) per row on every page view, which is correct but slow at scale. Option B: a comment_count column, updated with F('comment_count') + 1 inside the same transaction as the insert. Option B is fast, and it is correct as long as every code path that adds or removes comments goes through the same function.
In Django, use F() expressions for counters so the increment happens in the database and not in Python, which avoids lost updates when two requests increment at once.
The interview answer: 'I normalize to 3NF by default. I denormalize only for a measured read bottleneck or to keep historical facts, and I always name who keeps the copy consistent.'
keyPoints: Snapshot values that must not change retroactively (price, tax, address).
Summary tables / materialized views trade freshness for read speed.
Define refresh strategy, late-arriving data handling, and reconciliation.
Measure first; denormalize second.

sql.title: Materialized view for daily sales
sql.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales AS
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day,
       count(*)                      AS orders,
       sum(total_amount)             AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY 1;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON daily_sales(day);          -- required for CONCURRENTLY
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_sales;

django.title: Price snapshot on write
django.note: Django has no first-class materialized views; create them with migrations.RunSQL and read them through an unmanaged model (managed = False).

exercise: Design a daily_sales_summary table. State how it is refreshed, how late-arriving updates are handled, and how totals are reconciled against orders.
pitfalls: Denormalizing before measuring.
Counters kept in two places with no reconciliation job.
Computing historical invoices from the current catalogue price.

interview.q: When is denormalization justified?
interview.a: When measured read cost or an access pattern warrants it AND the team can manage consistency, update paths, reconciliation and ownership.

interview.q: How do you keep historical order totals correct?
interview.a: Snapshot unit price, discounts, tax and currency on order_items. Never derive past invoices from the current product price.

basis: Mid priority. Trade-off reasoning is a mid/senior signal.

title: Data Types
tagline: Pick types by meaning, range, precision and operations.
explain: Choosing a column type decides correctness, storage size, and which indexes work. Most type bugs are silent: they do not crash, they quietly store the wrong thing.
## Numbers

- INTEGER, BIGINT: whole numbers. Use BIGINT for ids that may pass about 2 billion. An INT primary key that overflows stops all inserts.
- NUMERIC(p, s) or DECIMAL: exact decimals. Use this for money.
- FLOAT, DOUBLE: binary approximations. Never use for money. 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in binary floating point, and the errors accumulate over thousands of rows.
- Store money as NUMERIC, or as integer minor units (cents) plus a currency code.
## Text

- VARCHAR(n) vs TEXT: in PostgreSQL they perform the same, and the limit is just a rule. Use VARCHAR(n) when the limit is a real business rule, otherwise TEXT.
- Compare with the right collation: case-insensitive comparison of emails needs lower() or a case-insensitive type, otherwise Bob@x.com and bob@x.com are two users.
- Do not put structured data in a text blob. Use proper columns or JSONB.
## Dates and time

- DATE: a calendar day. TIME: a clock time. TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE: a clock reading with no zone. TIMESTAMPTZ: an exact instant.
- Rule of thumb: store instants as TIMESTAMPTZ (UTC) and convert to the user's zone only when displaying. In Django set USE_TZ = True so datetimes are timezone-aware.
- Storing local times without a zone is how you get meetings that appear an hour early after a daylight-saving change.
## Booleans, enums, UUID, JSON

- BOOLEAN: true, false, or NULL. That third state surprises people (see below).
- Enum or a CHECK constraint on a small set of values, with Django's TextChoices on the model side.
- UUID: native type, not a 36-character string.
- JSONB (PostgreSQL): flexible semi-structured data that you can index. Good for optional attributes. Bad as a replacement for real columns you filter and join on every day.
## NULL is not a value

NULL means 'unknown'. Any comparison with NULL is itself unknown, not true: NULL = NULL is not true, and WHERE col != 'x' silently drops rows where col is NULL. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, and COALESCE(col, default) to supply a fallback. Prefer NOT NULL with a default whenever 'unknown' is not a real state, because every nullable column is one more case in every query.
> A discount column is NULL for 'no discount'. SELECT AVG(discount) ignores NULL rows and reports 10 percent, when across all orders the average is 2 percent. If 'no discount' means 0, store 0.
Interview favourites: float vs decimal for money, TIMESTAMP vs TIMESTAMPTZ, and what NULL does inside a WHERE clause or a NOT IN list.
keyPoints: Money → NUMERIC(12,2) (or integer minor units). Never float.
Instants → timestamptz (stores UTC, converts on display).
JSONB + GIN for flexible attributes; columns for anything you query constantly.
NULL is not a value: it propagates through comparisons (three-valued logic).

sql.title: Types chosen on purpose
sql.code:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id         BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  sku        TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  price      NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  discount   NUMERIC(5,2)  CHECK (discount BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
  active     BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
  attributes JSONB   NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

SELECT NULL = NULL;               -- NULL, not true
SELECT COALESCE(discount, 0) FROM products;

django.title: Field choices map to column types
django.code:
class Product(models.Model):
    sku = models.CharField(max_length=64, unique=True)          # varchar(64)
    price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=12, decimal_places=2) # numeric(12,2)
    attributes = models.JSONField(default=dict)                  # jsonb
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)         # timestamptz when USE_TZ=True
django.note: Never use FloatField for money. Keep USE_TZ = True so DateTimeField is timestamptz.

exercise: Choose types for price, discount %, stock quantity, order status, product attributes, birth date and created timestamp. Explain every choice in one sentence.
pitfalls: FLOAT for money (0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3).
timestamp without time zone for "when did it happen".
Storing everything in a JSONB blob and losing constraints and statistics.

interview.q: Why not store money as float?
interview.a: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly; errors accumulate. Use NUMERIC or integer minor units (paise/cents).

interview.q: timestamp vs timestamptz in PostgreSQL?
interview.a: timestamptz stores an absolute instant (normalized to UTC) and renders in the session time zone; timestamp stores a wall-clock reading with no zone and is usually wrong for events.

basis: Mid priority. Foundation for correct schemas.

title: Constraints
tagline: Make invalid states unrepresentable at the database boundary.
explain: A constraint is a rule the database itself enforces on every write, no matter which app, script, or person writes. Application validation can be bypassed by a bug, a second service, a bulk script, or a person in the SQL shell. Constraints cannot, so they are your last line of defence for data correctness.
## The constraint types

- NOT NULL: this column must have a value.
- UNIQUE: no two rows may share this value (or combination of values). Backed by an index.
- PRIMARY KEY: NOT NULL plus UNIQUE, and the row's identity.
- FOREIGN KEY: the value must exist in another table (see Keys).
- CHECK: an arbitrary condition on the row, such as price >= 0 or end_date > start_date.
- DEFAULT: not a restriction, but supplies a value when none is given.
- EXCLUDE (PostgreSQL): no two rows may overlap, which is how you prevent double-booking a room for overlapping time ranges.
## Why enforce in the database as well as in code

- Many writers: web app, admin, workers, imports, migrations. One rule in one place covers them all.
- Concurrency: two requests can both pass an app-level 'does this email exist?' check at the same moment, then both insert. Only a UNIQUE constraint closes that race.
- Trust: queries can assume the data is valid, so they need fewer defensive checks.

> Two users sign up with the same email in the same second. Both requests run User.objects.filter(email=...).exists(), both see False, both insert. Without a UNIQUE constraint you now have two accounts. With it, the second insert fails with an IntegrityError, which you catch and report as 'email already used'.
## Handling violations

A constraint failure raises an error you should expect and handle, not a bug to hide. In Django, catch django.db.IntegrityError around the write. Inside a transaction, a failed statement aborts the whole transaction in PostgreSQL, so wrap the risky write in its own atomic() block so the outer work can continue.
## Constraints in Django

Put them in Meta.constraints with CheckConstraint and UniqueConstraint, rather than relying on field options alone. UniqueConstraint supports conditions, so 'one active subscription per user' is expressed as unique on user where status = 'active'. Constraints are created by migrations, so adding one to a table with bad existing rows fails until you clean the data first.
Interview angle: 'why a constraint if you already validate in the serializer?' The answer is race conditions and multiple writers.
keyPoints: App validation = UX. DB constraints = truth.
CHECK (available_qty >= 0) is what finally prevents overselling.
UNIQUE(provider, provider_txn_id) gives payment idempotency for free.
Write positive AND negative constraint tests.

django.title: Meta.constraints
django.note: Catch django.db.IntegrityError in the service layer and map it to a 409 / 422 response.

exercise: Add constraints for non-negative price, unique email, positive order quantity, allowed status values, and one payment reference per provider transaction. Write a failing insert for each.

Adding a UNIQUE constraint to a table that already has duplicates (the migration fails).
Using a PostgreSQL ENUM for statuses that will change often.

interview.q: Why have DB constraints if the app already validates?
interview.a: Apps race, get bypassed by scripts, and multiple services write to the same DB. Constraints are the only check that is atomic with the write.

basis: Core. Integrity at the database boundary underpins transactions and idempotency.

title: SQL vs NoSQL
tagline: Choose by access pattern and consistency need, not by hype.
explain: 'SQL or NoSQL?' is not a contest. Each is a set of trade-offs, and good engineers choose by looking at the data and the access pattern. The default for most business applications is a relational database, and you move away from it when a specific need justifies it.
## What relational (SQL) gives you

- A fixed schema that rejects bad data, plus constraints and foreign keys.
- Joins: combine any tables in ways you did not plan in advance.
- ACID transactions across many rows and tables.
- A mature query language, tooling, and decades of operational knowledge.
The cost: scaling writes beyond one machine is hard (see Sharding), and schema changes on huge tables need care.
## The NoSQL families

- Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB): get or set by key, extremely fast, no rich queries. Fits caches, sessions, counters, rate limiting.
- Document (MongoDB): nested JSON-like documents, flexible schema. Fits data read as a whole unit, such as a product page with varied attributes.
- Wide-column (Cassandra): huge write volume spread over many machines, queried by a known key. Fits time series, event logs, messaging.
- Graph (Neo4j): relationships are the data. Fits social graphs, recommendations, fraud rings.
- Search (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch): full-text search and ranking. Usually a secondary copy beside the main database, not the source of truth.
## How to choose: ask these questions

- What are the access patterns? If you must answer unplanned questions with filters and joins, choose relational. If you only ever fetch by a known key, a key-value or document store is enough.
- How strict must consistency be? Money and inventory need transactions. A like counter can be slightly wrong.
- How big and how fast? One well-tuned PostgreSQL server handles far more than most teams assume, typically millions of rows with ease. Reach for distribution when you have measured a limit, not before.
- What does the team already run and understand? Operating an extra database has a real cost.

> Social app. Users, posts, follows: relational, because of constraints and joins. Feed cache per user: Redis. Full-text post search: Elasticsearch fed from the main database. Message firehose with billions of writes: Cassandra. A realistic system uses several stores, each for what it does best. This is called polyglot persistence.
## Myths worth correcting

- 'NoSQL is faster.' It is faster at the specific patterns it was designed for, and usually slower or impossible for others.
- 'NoSQL has no schema.' The schema moves into your application code, where it is harder to enforce.
- 'SQL does not scale.' It scales vertically very far, and with read replicas and careful design much further. PostgreSQL also has JSONB, so it can store flexible documents too.
Interview answer shape: state the access pattern and consistency need first, name the default (relational), then justify any exception with one concrete reason.
keyPoints: Orders / payments → relational (ACID, constraints).
Sessions, cache, rate limits → key-value (Redis).
Flexible documents → document store (or JSONB first!).
Relationship traversal → graph. Clickstream → wide-column / columnar.

# usage

interview.a: PostgreSQL as source of truth for orders, payments and inventory (transactions + constraints). Redis for cache/sessions/rate limiting. Add search (OpenSearch) or a document store only for a concrete need such as full-text relevance.

title: Query Execution Plans (EXPLAIN)
tagline: Stop guessing why a query is slow — read the plan.
explain: When a query is slow, guessing is useless. EXPLAIN shows the plan the database chose: how it will find the rows, in what order, and with what cost. EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and reports what really happened, including real timings. Reading plans is the core skill of query tuning.
## How to read a plan

A plan is a tree. The database runs it from the innermost, most indented node outward: leaves first. Each node reports an estimated cost, an estimated row count, and (with ANALYZE) actual time and actual rows.

- Seq Scan: read every row of the table. Fine for small tables or when you need most rows. A problem when you want few rows from a big table.
- Index Scan: walk an index to find matching rows, then fetch each row from the table.
- Index Only Scan: answer entirely from the index, without touching the table. Fastest, needs a covering index.
- Bitmap Heap Scan: collect many index matches first, then read the table pages in order. Common for medium selectivity.
- Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join: the three ways to join. Nested loop suits a few outer rows with an indexed inner lookup. Hash join builds a hash table of one side and suits large unsorted inputs. Merge join suits inputs already sorted on the join key.
- Sort, Aggregate, Limit: the operations done after the rows are found.
## What to look for

- Estimated rows vs actual rows. If the planner guessed 10 and the truth is 100,000, it chose a bad plan from bad statistics. Run ANALYZE to refresh statistics.
- A Seq Scan on a big table with a selective filter: you probably need an index on the filtered column.
- A Sort that spills to disk: not enough memory, or you could use an index that already returns rows in order.
- Many loops on an inner node: a nested loop doing thousands of lookups. Total time is time per loop multiplied by loops.
- Rows removed by filter that is far larger than rows returned: you are reading much and keeping little.

> Query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42. Plan A: Seq Scan on orders, Filter customer_id = 42, Rows Removed by Filter 999,990, 480 ms. After CREATE INDEX on orders(customer_id): Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx, 0.05 ms. The same query, because the planner can now jump straight to the matching rows.
## Things that surprise people

- The planner may correctly ignore your index when the query returns a large part of the table, because reading the whole table sequentially is cheaper than thousands of random index lookups.
- Wrapping an indexed column in a function, such as WHERE lower(email) = 'x', stops a plain index from being used. Create an index on the expression instead.
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes the query. For INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, wrap it in a transaction and roll back.
- Cost numbers are in arbitrary units, useful only for comparing plans, not as milliseconds.

In Django, queryset.explain() prints the plan of the query it would run, and with PostgreSQL it accepts analyze=True. Use it together with django-debug-toolbar to see the SQL your ORM code really produces.
keyPoints: EXPLAIN = estimate. EXPLAIN ANALYZE = runs it (wrap writes in BEGIN … ROLLBACK).
Estimated vs actual rows → statistics health (run ANALYZE).
Cost ≠ time. Compare buffers and actual time.
Change ONE thing, re-measure.

Trusting cost numbers across different queries.
Benchmarking once on a cold cache and drawing conclusions.

interview.q: What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE do?
interview.a: Executes the statement and reports actual runtime and row counts next to the estimates. It is not a harmless estimate — for writes use a transaction and roll back.

interview.q: How do you investigate a slow production query?
interview.a: Find the fingerprint and frequency (pg_stat_statements), inspect plan, actual rows, buffers, waits and locks, check statistics and parameter distribution, reproduce safely, change one thing, measure, and monitor.

title: Indexing
tagline: Trade storage and write cost for fast lookups and orderings.
explain: An index is a separate, sorted structure that lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, like the index at the back of a book. It makes reads faster and writes slower, so you create indexes for the queries you actually run, not for every column.
## How a B-tree index works

The default index type is a B-tree: a balanced tree of sorted keys. To find a value, the database starts at the root and follows a handful of pointers down to the right leaf, in about log N steps. A table of 10 million rows needs roughly 3 or 4 page reads to locate a key, instead of reading every row. Because the keys are sorted, it also supports range queries (between, greater than), ordering, and prefix matches.
## Index types you should know

- B-tree: equality, ranges, ORDER BY. The default and the right answer most of the time.
- Hash: equality only. Rarely better than B-tree.
- GIN: for values that contain many items, such as JSONB, arrays, and full-text search.
- GiST and SP-GiST: geometric data, ranges, nearest-neighbour.
- BRIN: tiny index for very large tables whose values are naturally ordered, such as an append-only timestamp.
- Partial index: indexes only the rows matching a condition, such as WHERE status = 'pending'. Small and fast.
- Expression index: indexes a computed value, such as lower(email).
## Composite indexes and the leftmost rule

An index on (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then by b within a, then by c within b. It can serve queries filtering on a; on a and b; on a, b and c. It cannot efficiently serve a query filtering only on b or c. So column order matters: put equality columns first, then the range or sort column last.

> Query: WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'paid' ORDER BY created_at DESC. A good index: (customer_id, status, created_at). The two equalities narrow the search, and the rows come out already sorted by created_at, so no sort step is needed.
Pick a query and see which index entries the database can reach directly:
@viz:composite-index
## Covering indexes

If the index contains every column the query needs, the database never touches the table (an index-only scan). In PostgreSQL you can add extra payload columns with INCLUDE. This is the fastest read path but makes the index bigger.
## The cost of indexes

- Every INSERT, UPDATE of an indexed column, and DELETE must also update every index on the table. Ten indexes on a hot table means ten extra writes per row.
- Indexes use disk and memory.
- Low-selectivity columns are poor candidates. An index on a boolean that splits the table 50/50 rarely helps, while a partial index on the rare value often does.
## A practical checklist

- Find the slow query first (slow query log, pg_stat_statements), then EXPLAIN it, then add the index, then EXPLAIN again to confirm it is used.
- Index foreign keys that you join or delete through.
- Drop indexes that are never used (pg_stat_user_indexes shows usage).
- In production create indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so writes are not blocked. In Django, use AddIndexConcurrently.
Interview staples: how a B-tree works, the leftmost-prefix rule, when an index is ignored, covering index, and why more indexes slow writes.

Partial / expression / covering indexes shrink and sharpen.
Planner may ignore an index: low selectivity, tiny table, stale stats, function on column.
Too many indexes slow every write.

interview.q: Why might PostgreSQL ignore an index?
interview.a: Low selectivity, small table, stale stats, expression or type mismatch, a function on the column, too many rows fetched, or a seq scan estimated cheaper.

interview.q: Why does composite index column order matter?
interview.a: A B-tree is sorted by the first column, then the second… so it supports leading-prefix predicates and matching sort orders. Put equality columns first, then range/ORDER BY columns.

interview.q: What is a covering index?
interview.a: An index containing every column a query needs (via INCLUDE), allowing an index-only scan when the visibility map says pages are all-visible.

interview.q: Why can too many indexes hurt?
interview.a: Every insert/update/delete must maintain each index; they consume disk and cache and increase vacuum work.

title: ACID Properties
explain: ACID is the promise a transactional database makes about a group of statements that must succeed or fail together. A transaction is that group. The classic example is a bank transfer: subtract from A and add to B must either both happen or neither happen.
## The four properties

- Atomicity: all or nothing. If any step fails, every step is undone (rolled back). You never see half a transfer.
- Consistency: a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state. Constraints, foreign keys and your own rules hold after it commits. Note that the database enforces the rules you declared; it cannot guess business rules you never wrote down.
- Isolation: transactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-finished work. How strictly is a setting (see Isolation Levels).
- Durability: once the database says committed, the data survives a crash or power loss.
## How the database delivers it

- Write-ahead log (WAL): before changing data files, the database appends the change to a sequential log and flushes it to disk. On commit it flushes the log. After a crash it replays the log to restore every committed change and discards uncommitted ones. This is how atomicity and durability work together.
- Locks or MVCC: provide isolation (see the next concepts).
Follow one committed change through a crash, then one that never committed:
@viz:wal

> BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT. If the server dies after the first update and before COMMIT, on restart the first update is rolled back. Money is never lost or created.
## Transactions in Django

By default, Django runs in autocommit mode: each statement commits on its own. To group statements use transaction.atomic(), as a decorator or a context manager. If an exception leaves the block, everything inside is rolled back. Nested atomic() blocks become savepoints, so an inner failure can roll back just the inner part. Setting ATOMIC_REQUESTS = True wraps every request in a transaction, which is simple but holds a transaction open for the whole request, so keep requests short.
## Common mistakes

- Doing slow work inside a transaction, such as calling an external API or sending an email. The transaction holds locks the whole time. Do slow work after commit.
- Assuming a rollback undoes side effects outside the database, such as an email already sent or a message already queued. Use transaction.on_commit() for those.
- Catching an exception inside atomic() and carrying on. After a database error inside a PostgreSQL transaction, the transaction is unusable until you roll back, so put the risky statement in its own atomic() block.
- Believing ACID means 'safe from concurrency problems'. Isolation level and locking decide that.
Interview angle: define all four with one example each, explain WAL in two sentences, and know that 'consistency' in ACID is not the same word as consistency in the CAP theorem or in replication.
keyPoints: Transaction = BEGIN … COMMIT/ROLLBACK; SAVEPOINT for partial rollback.
Check affected-row counts: an UPDATE that touched 0 rows is a business failure.
Idempotency keys make retries safe.
External side effects are outside ACID — design for unknown outcomes.

from django.db import transaction
from django.db.models import F

@transaction.atomic
def place_order(customer_id, product_id, qty, idem_key):
    updated = Inventory.objects.filter(
        product_id=product_id, available_qty__gte=qty
    ).update(available_qty=F("available_qty") - qty)
    if updated == 0:
        raise OutOfStock()

    order = Order.objects.create(customer_id=customer_id, status="pending")
    OrderItem.objects.create(order=order, product_id=product_id, quantity=qty,
                             unit_price=Product.objects.get(pk=product_id).price)

    # side effects only AFTER the commit succeeds
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_confirmation_email.delay(order.id))
    return order

Swallowing exceptions inside atomic() so it commits half-done work.
Ignoring affected-row counts.

interview.q: Explain ACID with an order example.
interview.a: Atomic: stock decrement + order + items commit together or not at all. Consistent: CHECK(qty>=0) and FKs hold after commit. Isolated: two buyers of the last unit cannot both succeed. Durable: once COMMIT returns, WAL guarantees the order survives a crash.

interview.q: How do you handle a payment provider timeout?
interview.a: Treat the outcome as unknown. Use the provider’s idempotency key/reference, persist payment state (pending/unknown), reconcile via webhook or status query, and never blindly charge again.

interview.q: What is idempotency in an API?
interview.a: Repeating the same request with the same key returns the original outcome instead of repeating side effects. Store key, request identity and result transactionally.

basis: Core. transaction.atomic and on_commit are standard senior Django topics.

title: Isolation Levels
tagline: Which concurrent effects can your transaction observe?
explain: Isolation answers a question: when two transactions run at the same time, what is each one allowed to see of the other? Perfect isolation is slow, so databases offer levels, and each level allows some specific anomalies in exchange for speed.
## The anomalies, defined

- Dirty read: you read a change another transaction has not committed yet. If it rolls back, you acted on data that never existed.
- Non-repeatable read: you read a row twice in one transaction and get different values, because another transaction committed a change between your reads.
- Phantom read: you run the same query twice and the second returns extra or missing rows, because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows.
- Lost update: two transactions read a value, both compute a new one, and the second write overwrites the first.
- Write skew: two transactions each read an overlapping set, each updates a different row based on what it read, and together they break a rule neither broke alone (two doctors both go off call because each saw the other still on call).
## The four SQL levels

- Read Uncommitted: dirty reads possible. PostgreSQL does not implement it, it behaves as Read Committed.
- Read Committed: no dirty reads. Each statement sees data committed before that statement began. The PostgreSQL default.
- Repeatable Read: the transaction sees one snapshot taken at its first statement. In PostgreSQL this also prevents phantoms, and a conflicting concurrent update makes one transaction fail with a serialization error that you must retry. MySQL InnoDB's default is this level.
- Serializable: the result is as if transactions ran one after another. PostgreSQL detects dangerous patterns and aborts one transaction, so your code must retry on failure.

> Two sessions at Read Committed. Session A: SELECT balance returns 100. Session B: UPDATE balance to 50 and COMMIT. Session A: SELECT balance again returns 50. That is a non-repeatable read, and it is allowed at this level. At Repeatable Read, A would still see 100 for its whole transaction.
## Choosing a level

Stay on the default (Read Committed) and fix specific problems with explicit locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE, see the next concept) or constraints. Go higher when a whole transaction needs a consistent view, such as a report that must add up. At Repeatable Read and Serializable, write the retry loop, because failures are normal behaviour at those levels, not exceptional.
## In Django

Django does not change the isolation level per query by default. You can set it for a connection in DATABASES OPTIONS (for PostgreSQL, isolation_level using psycopg's constants). For most Django work, you combine Read Committed with select_for_update() and constraints.
Interview staples: name the three anomalies, what the PostgreSQL default is, why Repeatable Read can throw a serialization error, and the difference between a dirty read and a non-repeatable read.
keyPoints: Dirty read: impossible in PostgreSQL.
Non-repeatable read: possible in READ COMMITTED.
Phantoms: prevented by PostgreSQL’s REPEATABLE READ (snapshot isolation).
Write skew: needs SERIALIZABLE (or explicit locks).
Serializable ⇒ write a retry loop.

SELECT available_qty FROM inventory
 WHERE product_id = 42;           -- 10

                                                    WHERE product_id = 42;  -- autocommit
SELECT available_qty FROM inventory

interview.q: READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL?
interview.a: RC: new snapshot per statement. RR: stable snapshot for the whole transaction, prevents non-repeatable reads and phantoms. SERIALIZABLE (SSI): detects dangerous dependency cycles and aborts one transaction, which the app must retry.

interview.q: Is a dirty read possible in PostgreSQL?
interview.a: No. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted but behaves like READ COMMITTED.

basis: Core. Seniors are expected to reason about consistency; isolation level is a recurring decision area.

title: Concurrency Control: Locks and MVCC
tagline: Readers never block writers — but writers still conflict.
explain: Concurrency control is how a database lets many transactions run at once without corrupting each other. There are two main tools: locks, which make others wait, and MVCC, which gives each transaction its own consistent view of the data so readers rarely wait at all.
## MVCC: multi-version concurrency control

When a row is updated, PostgreSQL does not overwrite it. It writes a new version of the row and marks the old version as superseded. Each transaction sees the versions that were valid at its snapshot. The consequence is the best-known rule of PostgreSQL: readers do not block writers, and writers do not block readers. Old versions that no transaction can see any more are cleaned up later by VACUUM. A transaction left open for hours stops that cleanup and bloats the table, which is why long idle transactions are a production problem.
@viz:mvcc
## Locks: where waiting is needed

MVCC does not stop two writers changing the same row. For that there are row locks. When a transaction updates or deletes a row, it holds a lock on that row until it commits or rolls back, and the second writer waits.

- Row-level locks: UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE lock the specific rows.
- Table-level locks: DDL such as ALTER TABLE takes stronger locks. Some schema changes block all reads and writes on the table while they run, which is why migrations on big tables need planning.
- Advisory locks: locks you name yourself, for application-level mutual exclusion, such as 'only one worker may run this job'.
## Pessimistic vs optimistic locking

- Pessimistic: assume conflict will happen, so lock first. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads a row and locks it so nobody else can change it until you finish. Right when conflicts are frequent and the cost of a failure is high, such as stock for a limited item.
- Optimistic: assume conflict is rare, do not lock, and check at write time that nothing changed. You keep a version column and write UPDATE ... SET qty = ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 7. If zero rows were updated, someone else got there first, and you retry. Right when conflicts are rare and holding locks would hurt throughput.

> Last item in stock. Two buyers both read stock = 1, both decide it is available, both subtract one: you sold two items you had one of (a lost update). Fix with pessimistic locking: inside a transaction, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the product row. The second buyer waits, then re-reads stock = 0 and is told it is sold out. Or fix atomically: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 1 AND stock > 0, and check how many rows changed.
## Deadlocks

A deadlock is a cycle: transaction A holds row 1 and wants row 2, while B holds row 2 and wants row 1. Neither can proceed. The database detects the cycle and aborts one transaction with an error. Prevention: always lock rows in the same order, keep transactions short, and be ready to retry the aborted one.
@viz:deadlock
## In Django

- select_for_update() adds FOR UPDATE and must run inside transaction.atomic(). Options: nowait=True fails immediately instead of waiting, skip_locked=True skips rows already locked (ideal for job queues), of=('self',) to lock only the main table in a join.
- F() expressions make the arithmetic happen in the database: Product.objects.filter(pk=1, stock__gt=0).update(stock=F('stock') - 1).
- For optimistic locking add a version field and filter on it in update().
Interview staples: how MVCC lets readers and writers coexist, FOR UPDATE vs optimistic versioning, what a deadlock is and how you prevent it, and what SKIP LOCKED is for.
keyPoints: Atomic conditional UPDATE is often enough; FOR UPDATE when you must read-then-decide.
Lock rows in a consistent order (e.g. ORDER BY product_id).
Keep transactions short; never wait on user input or HTTP inside one.
Hot rows (flash sale) serialize on their row lock — design around it.

interview.a: Readers use snapshots, writers create new row versions. It reduces reader-writer blocking but produces dead tuples needing vacuum, and does not eliminate write-write conflicts.

interview.q: What is a deadlock and how do you prevent it?

title: Replication
tagline: Copies for availability and read scale — not a backup.
explain: Replication means keeping copies of the same database on several machines. You do it for three reasons: availability (another copy takes over if one dies), read scaling (spread read queries across copies), and safety (a copy survives losing a machine or a data centre). It does not make writes faster.
## The usual setup: primary and replicas

One machine, the primary, accepts all writes. It records every change in its write-ahead log (WAL) and streams that log to one or more replicas, which replay it. Replicas serve read-only queries. If the primary fails, you promote a replica to be the new primary. This is called failover.
## Synchronous vs asynchronous

- Asynchronous: the primary commits and replies to the client right away, and ships the change to replicas afterwards. Fast, but if the primary dies before a change reaches any replica, that committed change is lost after failover. This is the common default.
- Synchronous: the primary waits for at least one replica to confirm before replying. No lost commits, but every write pays the network round trip, and if the replica is down, writes stall unless you configure fallback.
- A middle path is to require confirmation from one of several replicas.
## Replication lag and the trouble it causes

With asynchronous replication, a replica is always slightly behind the primary. Usually milliseconds, but under heavy write load or a slow network it can reach seconds or minutes. The classic symptom is read-your-own-writes failure:

> A user changes their profile name. The write goes to the primary. The page reloads and the read goes to a replica that has not received the change yet, so the user sees the old name and thinks the save failed. Fixes: read from the primary for a short time after a user writes; route 'important' reads to the primary; or record the WAL position of the write and only read from a replica that has reached it.
## Failover: where it goes wrong

- Promoting a lagging replica loses the unreplicated changes.
- Split brain: the old primary comes back and believes it is still the primary, so two machines accept writes and the data diverges. Real systems use a consensus or fencing mechanism so only one primary exists at a time.
- Applications must reconnect to the new primary. A connection pool or proxy that tracks the primary helps.
## Other topologies

- Multi-primary (multi-master): several machines accept writes. It needs conflict resolution, because two people can change the same row in two places. Powerful but complicated.
- Logical replication: replicates row changes by table rather than the raw log, useful for upgrades and for feeding other systems.
- Cascading replicas: a replica feeds other replicas to reduce load on the primary.
## In Django

Declare more than one entry in DATABASES (for example default and replica) and add a database router with db_for_read and db_for_write so reads go to the replica and writes to the primary. Remember that inside a transaction you usually want the primary, and that anything that must see a just-written row should read from the primary.
Interview staples: sync vs async trade-off, what replication lag is and how it shows up, what failover and split brain are, and why replicas help reads but not writes.
keyPoints: Replication ≠ backup. PITR = base backup + archived WAL.
Async: faster, may lose last commits. Sync: safer, couples availability.
Route reads by consistency need, not by default.
Failover risks: split-brain, lag, promotion of a stale replica.

Reading order status from a replica immediately after creating it.
Never testing a restore.

interview.q: Replication vs backup?
interview.a: Replication improves availability and read scale but copies deletes and corruption. Backups and WAL/PITR enable recovery to an earlier moment.

interview.q: Synchronous vs asynchronous replication?
interview.a: Sync waits for configured standby acknowledgement: less acknowledged-write loss, more latency and coupling. Async is faster but can lag and lose recent commits on failover.

interview.q: What are RPO and RTO?
interview.a: RPO = tolerable data-loss window; RTO = tolerable recovery time. Backup frequency, WAL archiving, replication mode and failover automation determine them.

interview.q: Recover from an accidental DELETE?
interview.a: Stop further damage, preserve evidence, restore a backup to a separate instance, replay WAL to just before the delete, validate, then extract/cut over.

basis: Mid priority at 0-5 yrs, core at 5+: read/write routers, failover and eventual consistency are senior Django topics.

title: Sharding
tagline: Split rows across nodes — the last resort, not the first.
explain: Sharding splits one large dataset across several database servers, so each server holds only a part, called a shard. Replication copies the same data to many machines; sharding divides different data between machines. You shard when a single primary can no longer handle the write volume or the data size, even after you have optimized queries, added indexes, and added replicas.
## Try these first

Sharding adds permanent complexity. Before it: add indexes, fix slow queries, add caching, scale the machine up (vertical scaling), add read replicas, archive old data, and consider partitioning a big table inside one database. Many systems never need sharding.
## Partitioning vs sharding

Partitioning splits one table into pieces, but they live in the same database server. It helps queries and maintenance (drop an old month instantly). Sharding spreads the pieces across several servers, which is what actually raises the ceiling on writes and storage.
## The shard key
Every row is routed to a shard using a shard key, such as user_id. Choosing the key is the most important decision, and it is hard to change later.

- Range sharding: shard 1 holds ids 1 to 1 million, shard 2 the next million. Simple, and range queries are easy, but new data piles onto the newest shard, creating a hotspot.
- Hash sharding: shard = hash(key) mod N. Spreads load evenly, but range queries must ask every shard, and changing N moves most of the data.
- Directory (lookup) sharding: a table maps each key to its shard. Flexible, but the lookup becomes a dependency and a possible bottleneck.
- Consistent hashing: keys and servers sit on a ring, so adding a server moves only a small share of keys. Used in distributed caches and many datastores.

> Shard by user_id, so all of one user's rows live together. 'Show my orders' touches one shard. But 'total sales today across all users' must ask every shard and merge the results. Shard by country instead and a country with most of your users becomes a hotspot. A good key has high cardinality, spreads load evenly, and matches your most common query.
Hash-mod routing has a hidden cost: changing the number of servers reshuffles almost every key. Consistent hashing fixes that. Add a server and compare.
@viz:hashring
## What you give up

- Joins and transactions across shards are hard or impossible. Either keep related data on the same shard or accept eventual consistency and design around it.
- Unique constraints and auto-increment ids are only unique per shard. You need globally unique ids, such as UUIDs or snowflake-style ids.
- Resharding (changing the number of shards) is a heavy operation. Plan for it with many small logical shards mapped onto few physical servers.
- Operations multiply: backups, migrations, and monitoring per shard.
## In Django

Django can talk to several databases and route with a database router, so you can implement shard routing, but it gives you no built-in sharding and no cross-shard joins. Most teams use managed sharded databases or a tool such as Citus for PostgreSQL rather than hand-rolling it.

Interview staples: shard vs replica vs partition, how to choose a shard key, hotspots, and how to handle cross-shard queries. In system design answers, always say you would scale vertically, add replicas and caching first, and shard only when the numbers demand it.
keyPoints: Order of escalation: index → pool → vertical → partition → replicas → shard.
Shard key: high cardinality, even, aligned with queries.
Cross-shard queries/transactions are the cost you pay.
Plan rebalancing before day one.

interview.q: Partitioning vs sharding?
interview.a: Partitioning divides a table within one database/cluster. Sharding distributes data across independent database nodes and adds routing and coordination complexity.

interview.q: How do you choose a shard key?
interview.a: Query locality, cardinality, even distribution, tenant/customer boundaries, growth, hotspot risk and the cost of cross-shard operations.

interview.q: When should you shard?
interview.a: Only after measuring and exhausting indexing, query redesign, pooling, vertical scale, partitioning and replicas — and after quantifying the operational cost.

title: Consistency Models
tagline: State the guarantee each feature actually needs.
explain: Consistency models describe what a reader is guaranteed to see when data is stored on more than one machine, or both in a database and in a cache. Strong guarantees are easier to reason about and cost latency and availability. Weak guarantees are fast and available and push complexity onto you.
## The main models

- Strong (linearizable) consistency: once a write completes, every later read, anywhere, sees it. Behaves like a single copy. Needs coordination between machines, so it is slower and can become unavailable during network failures.
- Eventual consistency: if no new writes arrive, all copies converge to the same value eventually. Reads in the meantime may return older data. Fast and highly available.
- Read-your-writes: you always see your own writes, even if others do not yet.
- Monotonic reads: you never see data go backwards in time between two reads.
- Causal consistency: if one event causes another (a reply to a post), everyone sees them in that order.
## The CAP theorem and PACELC

CAP says that during a network partition (some machines cannot talk to others), a distributed system must choose between consistency (refuse or delay some requests to stay correct) and availability (keep answering, possibly with stale data). It does not say you only get two of three in normal operation. PACELC extends it: even without a partition, there is a trade-off between latency and consistency. Strong consistency costs round trips.

> A bank balance must not be stale: choose consistency, accept that some requests fail during a partition. A video view counter or a social feed can be a few seconds stale: choose availability and eventual consistency.
## Consistency in everyday backends: the cache
The most common place you meet this is a cache in front of a database. The cache and the database are two copies, and you must keep them in step.

- Cache-aside: read from cache, on a miss read the database and fill the cache. On a write, update the database and delete the cache entry. Deleting is safer than updating the cache.
- Write-through: write to the cache and the database together. Simple, but writes pay both costs.
- Write-behind: write to the cache and flush to the database later. Fast, but you can lose data on a crash.
- TTL (time to live): every entry expires after some time, which bounds how stale it can be. Always set one.
@viz:cache-aside
## The stale-cache race

Even cache-aside can go wrong. Reader A misses the cache and reads the old value from the database. Meanwhile writer B updates the database and deletes the cache entry. Then A writes its old value into the cache. The cache now holds stale data until the TTL expires. This is why TTLs matter, and why for critical data you read from the database. Another danger is a cache stampede: a popular key expires and hundreds of requests hit the database at once. Mitigate with a lock around the rebuild, jittered TTLs, or refreshing before expiry.
## In Django

Use the cache framework with Redis: cache.get, cache.set with a timeout, and cache.delete on writes. Delete cached entries in transaction.on_commit() so you never invalidate before the database change is visible. For data you can regenerate, a short TTL is often the simplest correct answer.
Interview staples: strong vs eventual consistency with an example of each, CAP stated correctly, cache-aside with its race condition, and stampede mitigation.
keyPoints: Per-feature consistency table: price, stock, order status, feed, counters.
Read-your-writes: after a write, route that user to the primary / bypass cache.
Monotonic reads: never show a user older data than they already saw.
Invalidate cache in transaction.on_commit.

sql.code:
-- primary, after commit
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();            -- 0/3000148

-- replica: has it replayed that point yet?
SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= '0/3000148'::pg_lsn AS caught_up;

django.title: Invalidate after commit
django.code:
def update_price(product_id, new_price):
    with transaction.atomic():
        Product.objects.filter(pk=product_id).update(price=new_price)
        # delete cache only once the new price is visible to other connections
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: cache.delete(f"product:{product_id}"))
django.note: Invalidating inside the transaction before commit lets another request re-cache the OLD value — a classic stale-cache bug.

exercise: Classify product price, inventory, order status, recommendation feed and analytics counters. Define stale-read tolerance and recovery behaviour for each.
pitfalls: Invalidating the cache before the transaction commits.
Calling everything "eventually consistent" without a staleness bound.
Cache stampede on a hot key after expiry.

interview.q: What is eventual consistency?
interview.a: Replicas or derived views converge after propagation; clients may briefly see stale data. Define the acceptable staleness and user-visible behaviour.

interview.q: What is replication lag and why does it matter?
interview.a: A replica may not yet contain a recent commit. Read-after-write flows should use the primary or wait/route based on the consistency needed.

interview.q: How would you cache product data safely?
interview.a: Cache-aside with TTL, invalidate on write after commit, version keys or short TTL for correctness, stampede protection (lock / single-flight), and fall back to the DB if Redis is down.

basis: Mid priority at 0-5 yrs, core at 5+: caching, invalidation and eventual consistency.

title: Django ORM in Depth
tagline: Lazy querysets, N+1, F/Q, annotate, and safe migrations: what Django interviews probe first.
explain: The ORM lets you write database queries as Python. It is convenient, and it hides the SQL, which is where most Django performance bugs come from. The goal of this lesson is to always know what SQL your code produces and how many queries it runs.
## QuerySets are lazy

A QuerySet is lazy: building it runs no SQL. The query executes when you iterate it, call list(), len() or bool() on it, or call .get(), .count() or .exists(). The results are cached on that QuerySet object, so iterating it twice hits the database once. But chaining another .filter() creates a new QuerySet and a new query.

> orders = Order.objects.filter(status='paid')   # no query yet
for o in orders: ...                              # one query runs here
len(orders)                                       # uses the cache, no new query
orders.count()                                    # runs a new SELECT COUNT(*)
If you only need to know whether any row exists, use .exists(), which stops at the first match. len(qs) loads every row into memory just to count them.
## The N+1 problem

The classic production bug: one query fetches a list, then one extra query runs per row whenever you touch a related object in a loop. Templates and serializers do this silently. With 100 orders, printing order.customer.name in a loop runs 101 queries.

- select_related() follows foreign keys and one-to-one links with a SQL JOIN, in a single query. Use it for 'the one related object'.
- prefetch_related() runs one extra query per relation and joins in Python. Use it for reverse foreign keys and many-to-many, where a JOIN would multiply rows.
- Prefetch() lets you filter or order the prefetched rows, or store them under a custom attribute.

> Order.objects.select_related('customer').prefetch_related('items__product')
This is 3 queries in total (orders joined with customers, then items, then products), no matter how many orders there are.
## Push work into the database

- F() expressions: refer to a column inside the query. update(stock=F('stock') - 1) is one atomic UPDATE with no read-modify-write race.
- Q() objects: build OR and NOT conditions, as in Q(status='paid') | Q(total__gt=1000).
- annotate() with Count, Sum or Avg: a per-row aggregate, which is a GROUP BY. aggregate() returns a single summary dictionary for the whole set.
- values() and values_list(): fetch only the columns you need, as dictionaries or tuples, skipping model object creation.
- only() and defer(): load a model but skip heavy columns.
- update(), bulk_create() and bulk_update() are single statements, but they skip save() overrides and signals.
## Migrations

A migration is a Python file that records a schema change. makemigrations writes it from your model changes and migrate applies it. Treat migrations as production code. Never edit one that has already been applied anywhere. On a big table, adding a column with a default, or an index without CONCURRENTLY, can lock the table, so add the column as nullable, backfill in batches, then add the constraint. Use RunPython with a reverse function for data changes, and keep schema and data migrations separate.
## See under the hood

str(qs.query) shows the SQL, qs.explain() shows the plan, django-debug-toolbar shows the query count per page, and assertNumQueries in a test locks the count in so a regression fails the build. When the ORM cannot express a query, use raw() or a cursor with parameters (%s placeholders, never f-strings).
keyPoints: QuerySets are lazy and cached; .exists() and .count() beat len(qs) when you do not need the rows.
N+1 = 1 + N queries. select_related = JOIN (single-valued relations); prefetch_related = extra query (multi-valued).
F() updates atomically in the database; Q() builds OR/NOT; annotate() = GROUP BY per row; aggregate() = one result.
update() and bulk_*() skip save() and signals.
Measure, do not guess: qs.query, qs.explain(), assertNumQueries.

-- produces roughly:
SELECT o.id, COUNT(i.product_id) AS n_items, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS total
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.id;

-- Inventory.objects.filter(product_id=42, available_qty__gte=1).update(available_qty=F("available_qty") - 1)
UPDATE inventory
   SET available_qty = available_qty - 1
