django.title: Fix N+1, prove it, push work to the database, migrate safely
django.code:
from django.db import migrations, models
from django.db.models import F, Q, Count, Sum, Prefetch
from django.contrib.postgres.operations import AddIndexConcurrently

# 1) N+1 and the fix
for o in Order.objects.all()[:20]:
    print(o.customer.full_name)                 # 1 + 20 queries

orders = (Order.objects
          .select_related("customer")                                                      # JOIN
          .prefetch_related(Prefetch("items", queryset=OrderItem.objects.select_related("product")))
          [:20])                                                                           # 2 queries total

# 2) make N+1 a failing test, not a production incident
class OrderListTests(TestCase):
    def test_query_count_is_constant(self):
        with self.assertNumQueries(2):
            list(orders_for_list())

# 3) let the database do the work
Inventory.objects.filter(product_id=42, available_qty__gte=1).update(available_qty=F("available_qty") - 1)
Product.objects.filter(Q(active=True) & (Q(price__lt=500) | Q(name__icontains="sale")))
Order.objects.annotate(n_items=Count("items"), total=Sum(F("items__quantity") * F("items__unit_price")))

# 4) index a big table without blocking writes
class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    atomic = False                                # CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction
    operations = [AddIndexConcurrently("product", models.Index(fields=["category", "-created_at"], name="idx_prod_cat_created"))]
django.note: Put assertNumQueries on every list endpoint. It turns an N+1 into a failing test instead of a slow production page. Test against PostgreSQL where you can; SQLite hides locking and planner behaviour.

exercise: Take a view that lists 20 orders with the customer name and each order's items. Count the queries (debug toolbar or assertNumQueries) before and after fixing it with select_related and prefetch_related, then write the test that locks the count in. Finally add a composite index with AddIndexConcurrently and show with qs.explain() that it is used.
pitfalls: Touching related objects in a loop, template or serializer without select_related/prefetch_related.
Calling .filter() on an already-prefetched relation: it ignores the prefetch cache and queries again. Use Prefetch(queryset=…) instead.
Using len(qs) or bool(qs) just to check for rows: use .exists() / .count().
Read-modify-write in Python (obj.qty -= 1; obj.save()) instead of F(): lost updates under concurrency.
Expecting update(), bulk_create() or bulk_update() to run save() overrides or signals.
Adding a column with a default, or backfilling millions of rows, in one migration on a live table.

interview.q: select_related vs prefetch_related?
interview.a: select_related does a SQL JOIN and loads the related row in the same query; it works for ForeignKey and OneToOne (single-valued). prefetch_related issues a separate query per relation and stitches the results together in Python; use it for reverse foreign keys and many-to-many, or when a JOIN would multiply rows. Prefetch() lets you filter or order the prefetched queryset.

interview.q: How do you find and fix an N+1 problem in Django?
interview.a: Detect it with django-debug-toolbar, query logging, or assertNumQueries in a test. Fix it by loading what you will touch up front: select_related for FK/one-to-one, prefetch_related for the rest. Then lock the query count in with assertNumQueries so it cannot regress.

interview.q: get() vs filter()?
interview.a: get() returns exactly one object and raises DoesNotExist if none or MultipleObjectsReturned if several. filter() returns a QuerySet that may be empty and is lazy. Use get_object_or_404 in views.

interview.q: Explain QuerySet laziness and caching.
interview.a: Creating or chaining a QuerySet runs no SQL; it executes on iteration, list(), len(), bool(), get(), count() or exists(). Once evaluated, results are cached on that object, so iterating again does not re-query, but a new .filter() builds a new QuerySet and queries again.

interview.q: update() vs save() on a model?
interview.a: update() on a QuerySet issues one UPDATE statement, returns the number of rows changed, and skips save() overrides and pre/post_save signals. save() works on one instance, runs the override and signals, and writes all fields unless you pass update_fields.

interview.q: What is an F() expression and why use it?
interview.a: F() refers to a column value inside the database, e.g. update(qty=F('qty') - 1). The calculation happens in one atomic UPDATE, so concurrent requests cannot overwrite each other the way a Python read-modify-write can.

interview.q: annotate() vs aggregate()?
interview.a: aggregate() collapses the whole queryset to one dict of values (e.g. total revenue). annotate() adds a computed value to each row, which with Count/Sum becomes a GROUP BY (e.g. item count per order).

interview.q: How do you add an index to a large table in production without blocking writes?
interview.a: Use AddIndexConcurrently from django.contrib.postgres.operations in a migration with atomic = False, which runs CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Backfill data in batches in a separate step.

basis: Core. select_related/prefetch_related, F and Q objects, aggregation and migrations are the standard mid-level Django ORM topics; N+1, indexing and zero-downtime migrations appear at senior level.

title: Django REST Framework & API Design
tagline: Serializers, viewsets, permissions, pagination, and idempotent writes.
explain: Django REST Framework (DRF) turns Django models into HTTP APIs. It is built from a few layers, and knowing what each layer does lets you drop down a level when the magic gets in your way.
## Serializers

A serializer does two jobs: it validates incoming data (deserialization) and shapes outgoing data (serialization). ModelSerializer generates fields and validators from a model. Add field-level validation with validate_<field>() and cross-field rules with validate(). Keep business rules out of the serializer where possible and in a service function, so they work from the API, the admin and management commands alike.

> class OrderSerializer(ModelSerializer):
    class Meta: model = Order; fields = ['id', 'items', 'total']; read_only_fields = ['total']
Marking total read-only means a client can send any number and it is ignored. Never trust a client-sent price or status.
## Views: three layers

- APIView: you write get, post and so on yourself. Full control.
- Generic views (ListCreateAPIView and friends): mixins that provide the common list, create, retrieve, update and delete behaviour.
- ViewSet plus a Router: full CRUD from one class and automatic URLs. Least code, most magic.
## Authentication and permissions

Authentication answers who you are (session, token, or JWT through a third-party package). Permissions answer whether you may do this. IsAuthenticated protects the view, but the bug that ships to production is the missing object-level check: any logged-in user can fetch /orders/123. Fix it by filtering get_queryset() by request.user, or by implementing has_object_permission. Throttling limits request rates per user, IP or scope.
## List endpoints

- Pagination: page-number and limit/offset pagination use SQL OFFSET and get slower on deep pages, because the database must skip all earlier rows. Cursor pagination uses a keyset (WHERE id < last_seen ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT n) so it stays fast and stable while rows are inserted.
- Filtering and ordering: allow only a list of named fields, never arbitrary columns.
- Query tuning: serializers are the most common place N+1 hides, so build the queryset in get_queryset() with select_related and prefetch_related.
## Write endpoints

- Validate in the serializer and keep business rules in a service function inside transaction.atomic().
- Return consistent status codes: 400 validation error, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 429 throttled.
- PUT replaces the whole resource, PATCH changes part of it.
- Make POSTs that create valuable things idempotent with an Idempotency-Key header, so a retry after a timeout cannot create a duplicate order.
- Version your API (a URL prefix such as /api/v1/) before clients depend on it.
keyPoints: Serializer = validation + representation; ModelSerializer generates both from the model.
APIView → generic views → ViewSet + Router: less code, more magic.
Authentication ≠ authorization. Object-level checks prevent IDOR.
Cursor pagination for big or fast-changing lists; allowlist ordering and filter fields.
N+1 hides in serializers: optimise get_queryset().
PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates; Idempotency-Key makes POST retry-safe.

sql.title: Offset versus cursor (keyset) pagination
sql.code:
-- Offset: the database reads and discards 100,000 rows to return 20
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;

-- Cursor / keyset: start after the last row you returned; an index on (created_at, id) makes it cheap
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-11-01 10:00:00+00', 98765)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

sql.title: Idempotency keys
sql.code:
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key             TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
  request_hash    TEXT NOT NULL,
  response_status INTEGER,
  response_body   JSONB,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING;  0 rows inserted -> a retry: return the stored response

django.title: A safe, fast list endpoint
django.code:
from rest_framework import serializers, viewsets, filters
from rest_framework.pagination import CursorPagination
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from rest_framework.throttling import ScopedRateThrottle

class OrderSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    items = OrderItemSerializer(many=True, read_only=True)
    class Meta:
        model = Order
        fields = ["id", "status", "total_amount", "created_at", "items"]   # explicit, never "__all__"
        read_only_fields = ["status", "total_amount"]                       # the client may not set these

class OrderPagination(CursorPagination):
    page_size = 20
    ordering = ("-created_at", "-id")                                       # stable, indexed ordering

class OrderViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = OrderSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]
    pagination_class = OrderPagination
    filter_backends = [filters.OrderingFilter]
    ordering_fields = ["created_at", "total_amount"]                        # allowlist
    throttle_classes = [ScopedRateThrottle]
    throttle_scope = "orders"                                               # rate set in REST_FRAMEWORK["DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES"]

    def get_queryset(self):
        return (Order.objects
                .filter(customer__user=self.request.user)                   # object-level isolation: no IDOR
                .select_related("customer")
                .prefetch_related("items__product"))                        # no N+1 inside the serializer
django.note: For POST /orders, read the Idempotency-Key header, look it up in your idempotency table inside the same transaction, and return the stored response on a repeat. The serializer should never accept price, status or total from the client.

exercise: Build GET /orders with cursor pagination, an ordering allowlist and object-level isolation, and a test using assertNumQueries that proves the query count does not grow with the number of orders. Then build POST /orders with an Idempotency-Key and test that sending it twice returns the same order and creates only one.
pitfalls: fields = "__all__" leaking internal columns or allowing mass assignment.
Checking IsAuthenticated but never filtering objects by owner (IDOR).
Nested serializers or SerializerMethodField running a query per row.
Offset pagination on large tables; ordering by a non-unique field with cursor pagination.
Letting clients order or filter by any field.
Trusting the client for price, total or status; returning 200 with an error body.

interview.q: What does a DRF serializer do?
interview.a: It validates incoming data (deserialization) and converts model instances to primitive types for the response (serialization). ModelSerializer generates fields and validators from a model; validate_<field>() and validate() add custom rules.

interview.q: APIView vs generic views vs ViewSets?
interview.a: APIView gives you raw HTTP method handlers. Generic views add reusable mixins (list, create, retrieve…). ViewSets group related actions into one class and a Router generates the URLs. Moving up the stack means less code and less visibility; drop down when you need custom behaviour.

interview.q: Authentication vs permissions in DRF?
interview.a: Authentication identifies the caller (session, token, JWT via a package). Permissions decide if that caller may perform the action (IsAuthenticated, custom classes, has_object_permission). Both run before the view body.

interview.q: How do you prevent one user reading another user's data (IDOR)?
interview.a: Authorize the object, not just the user: filter get_queryset() by the owner (e.g. customer__user=request.user) so other people's objects return 404, or implement has_object_permission, and test it with two users.

interview.q: Why prefer cursor pagination over offset?
interview.a: OFFSET makes the database scan and discard all earlier rows, so deep pages get slow, and inserts between requests cause skipped or duplicated items. Cursor (keyset) pagination filters from the last seen value using an index, so it stays fast and stable. It needs a stable, unique ordering.

interview.q: How do you avoid N+1 in DRF?
interview.a: Build the queryset in get_queryset() with select_related / prefetch_related for everything the serializer touches, and lock the count with assertNumQueries.

interview.q: PUT vs PATCH?
interview.a: PUT replaces the whole resource and expects all required fields; PATCH applies a partial update (serializer partial=True).

interview.q: How do you make POST /orders safe to retry?
interview.a: Require an Idempotency-Key header, store key + request hash + response in the same transaction as the order, and on a repeat return the stored response instead of creating another order. A unique constraint on the key protects against concurrent duplicates.

basis: Core for Django roles. Serializers, viewsets, routers, filtering and pagination are in the Middle (3-5 yrs) Django topic list; API design is the mid-level focus.

title: Celery & Background Jobs
tagline: Move slow work out of the request, and survive retries, crashes and the on_commit race.
explain: Anything slow or unreliable, such as sending email, calling a payment API, generating a PDF or resizing an image, should not run inside the web request. The user waits, a slow third party ties up your web workers, and a failure becomes a failed page. Celery moves that work out of the request into a background worker.
## How it fits together

- Producer: your Django app calls task.delay(args). That publishes a message (the task name and its arguments) to a broker.
- Broker: a queue such as Redis or RabbitMQ that holds messages until a worker takes one.
- Worker: a separate process that consumes messages and runs your task function. Run more workers to process more at once.
- Result backend: optional storage for return values. You only need it if you read results back.
- Beat: a scheduler process that enqueues periodic tasks, such as nightly reports and cleanup.
Follow one message through the system, then see what happens when the worker dies.
@viz:celery-flow
## Delivery is at-least-once

By default a task is acknowledged just before it runs, so a worker crash mid-task can lose it. With acks_late the message is redelivered after a crash, and may then run twice. Either way you cannot assume exactly once, so write idempotent tasks: make the effect safe to repeat, with a unique constraint or a 'processed' marker. This is the same idea as an Idempotency-Key. Also pass IDs, not model instances, and re-load fresh data inside the task, because the object may have changed or been deleted by the time it runs.
## The race that bites everyone
If you call .delay() inside transaction.atomic(), the worker can pick the task up before your transaction commits, then fail with DoesNotExist because the row is not visible yet.

> with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.create(...)
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.delay(order.id))
The task is only queued after COMMIT succeeds, and not at all if the transaction rolls back. If even that is not enough (the process can crash between COMMIT and the enqueue), use the outbox pattern: write a to-do row in the same transaction, and let a separate publisher send it.
## Failure is a normal case

- Retries: autoretry_for with retry_backoff and jitter, and a max_retries cap so a poison task cannot loop forever.
- Time limits: soft and hard limits so a hung task does not hold a worker forever.
- Separate queues: keep slow, bulk work apart from urgent work such as password-reset emails.
- Monitoring: watch queue length and failure rate. A silently backed-up queue is an outage that nobody noticed.
keyPoints: Web app → broker (Redis/RabbitMQ) → worker. Result backend only if you need results.
At-least-once delivery means tasks must be idempotent.
Pass IDs and re-load inside the task; never pass model instances.
Enqueue with transaction.on_commit(); outbox pattern when you cannot lose the job.
Retries: backoff + jitter + max_retries; add time limits.
Monitor queue depth and failures.

sql.title: Idempotent effect: do it once even if the task runs twice
sql.code:
CREATE TABLE points_ledger (
  order_id   BIGINT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES orders(id),   -- one row per order, enforced by the database
  points     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
INSERT INTO points_ledger (order_id, points) VALUES (42, 10)
ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO NOTHING;      -- a retry or duplicate delivery inserts 0 rows and changes nothing

sql.title: Outbox pattern
sql.code:
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id         BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  task       TEXT  NOT NULL,
  payload    JSONB NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  sent_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
);
-- INSERT the row in the SAME transaction as the order. A publisher then claims unsent rows:
SELECT id, task, payload FROM outbox
WHERE sent_at IS NULL
ORDER BY id
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 50;

django.title: Idempotent task, enqueued after commit
django.code:
# orders/tasks.py
from celery import shared_task
from django.db import OperationalError, transaction

@shared_task(bind=True, autoretry_for=(OperationalError,), retry_backoff=True, retry_jitter=True,
             max_retries=5, soft_time_limit=30)
def award_points(self, order_id):                      # pass the ID, not the Order
    with transaction.atomic():
        PointsLedger.objects.get_or_create(order_id=order_id, defaults={"points": 10})   # unique(order_id)
    # a retry or duplicate delivery finds the row and does nothing

# orders/services.py
@transaction.atomic
def place_order(customer, cart):
    order = Order.objects.create(customer=customer, status="pending")
    ...
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: award_points.delay(order.id))   # enqueue only after COMMIT
django.note: For effects outside your database (an email, a payment call) a unique row cannot make the effect itself idempotent. Use the provider's idempotency key where it exists, or accept at-least-once delivery and design the message so a duplicate is harmless.

exercise: Add a Celery task that awards points once per order. Prove with a test that calling the task twice for the same order creates one ledger row. Then deliberately call .delay() inside atomic() with a worker running and watch the DoesNotExist race, and fix it with transaction.on_commit.
pitfalls: Calling .delay() inside transaction.atomic() (the worker runs before the COMMIT).
Passing model instances or non-serializable arguments instead of IDs.
Assuming exactly-once execution; non-idempotent tasks that double-charge or double-email.
Retrying forever with no backoff, no max_retries and no time limit.
No monitoring of queue length; running multiple Beat instances and double-scheduling.

interview.q: Why and how would you use Celery in a Django app?
interview.a: To move slow or unreliable work (email, payments, reports) out of the request cycle. Django publishes a message to a broker (Redis/RabbitMQ), workers consume and execute it; a result backend is optional. It improves response time and lets you retry and schedule work.

interview.q: Why use transaction.on_commit with Celery?
interview.a: If you enqueue inside atomic(), the worker may run before the transaction commits and not find the row (DoesNotExist). on_commit runs the callback only after a successful COMMIT, so the data is visible. If the process may crash between commit and enqueue, use an outbox table.

interview.q: What happens if a Celery task runs twice?
interview.a: It can: delivery is at-least-once, especially with acks_late or after a worker crash or retry. Make tasks idempotent, for example with a unique constraint or a processed marker, so a repeat is harmless.

interview.q: How do you configure retries with backoff?
interview.a: Use autoretry_for for the exception types, retry_backoff=True (optionally retry_jitter), and a max_retries cap; add soft_time_limit/time_limit so a stuck task cannot hang a worker.

interview.q: What should you pass as Celery task arguments?
interview.a: Small, JSON-serializable values such as IDs. Re-load the object inside the task so you act on current data and avoid serializing stale model instances.

interview.q: Celery Beat vs cron?
interview.a: Beat is Celery's scheduler: it enqueues periodic tasks that workers execute, with schedules defined in config or the database. Run exactly one Beat instance or tasks will be scheduled twice; cron is simpler for a single host with no queue.

interview.q: How do you make sure an event is not lost if the app crashes right after commit?
interview.a: The transactional outbox: insert an outbox row in the same transaction as the business change, and have a publisher read unsent rows (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) and enqueue them, marking them sent.

basis: Mid priority at 0-5 yrs, core at 5+. Celery setup, Beat and retries with backoff are Senior Django topics, junior roles ask only for basic awareness, and on_commit before enqueueing is a named senior topic.

title: Web Security for Django APIs
tagline: What Django protects by default, how people switch it off, and the bug that is not in the framework: access control.
explain: Django is secure by default in several places, if you do not switch the protection off. Most real vulnerabilities come from stepping outside those defaults. Learn what is protected for you and what is not.
## What Django protects by default

- SQL injection: the ORM sends parameters separately from the SQL text, so queries built with filter() are not injectable.
- XSS (cross-site scripting): templates auto-escape variables, which blocks most XSS.
- CSRF (cross-site request forgery): CsrfViewMiddleware rejects state-changing requests from a browser that lack a valid token.
- Clickjacking: XFrameOptionsMiddleware sets X-Frame-Options so other sites cannot frame your pages.
- Passwords: stored as salted, slow hashes (PBKDF2 by default), never plaintext.
## How people break out of the defaults

- Raw SQL built with f-strings or % formatting. Always pass parameters: cursor.execute('... WHERE id = %s', [value]).
- mark_safe() or the |safe filter on user input, which switches auto-escaping off.
- @csrf_exempt on views that use cookie authentication.
- DEBUG=True in production, which leaks settings and stack traces, or a leaked SECRET_KEY, which lets an attacker forge sessions and signed data.
- An over-permissive ALLOWED_HOSTS, or CORS_ALLOW_ALL_ORIGINS together with credentials.

> Bad: User.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE username = '{name}'")
Sending name = "x' OR '1'='1" returns every user. Good: User.objects.raw('SELECT * FROM auth_user WHERE username = %s', [name]), where the value is sent separately and never parsed as SQL.
## Broken access control: the bug the framework cannot catch

IDOR (insecure direct object reference) means /orders/123 works for any logged-in user, not only its owner. Authentication proves who someone is. Every object access also needs an authorization check: filter the queryset by request.user, or verify ownership before returning or changing data. This is one of the most common API flaws, because it is easy to forget and every test as the owner still passes.
## CORS vs CSRF, and going to production

CSRF protects cookie-authenticated browsers from cross-site form posts. CORS decides which other origins may read your API's responses from JavaScript. They are different problems and one does not replace the other. For production:

- Serve over HTTPS and set SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE and HSTS.
- Keep secrets in environment variables, never in the repository.
- Set DEBUG=False and a strict ALLOWED_HOSTS.
- Rate-limit login and other abusable endpoints.
- Run python manage.py check --deploy, which lists missing hardening settings.
- Keep Django and dependencies updated, because security fixes ship as patch releases.
keyPoints: ORM parameters prevent SQL injection; raw SQL must use %s parameters, never f-strings.
Auto-escaping blocks XSS; mark_safe on user input defeats it.
CSRF token = proof the request came from your own page; CORS controls cross-origin reads.
Authentication ≠ authorization: check object ownership (IDOR).
Never ship DEBUG=True or a committed SECRET_KEY; run check --deploy.

--   SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1';     -- returns every customer

-- Safe: the value travels separately from the statement
PREPARE find_customer(text) AS
  SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = $1;
EXECUTE find_customer($$' OR '1'='1$$);                      -- treated as an ordinary string, matches nothing

django.title: Injection, IDOR and production settings
django.code:
# SQL injection: never format user input into SQL
Customer.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = '{email}'")     # VULNERABLE
Customer.objects.raw("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = %s", [email])    # safe: parameters
Customer.objects.filter(email=email)                                         # safest: the ORM

# IDOR: authorize the object, not just the user
def order_detail(request, pk):
    order = get_object_or_404(Order, pk=pk, customer__user=request.user)     # someone else's order -> 404
    return JsonResponse(serialize(order))

# settings for production
DEBUG = False
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["api.example.com"]
SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000
# then run:  python manage.py check --deploy
django.note: Run check --deploy in CI so a risky setting fails the build. Returning 404 (not 403) for other people's objects avoids confirming that the object exists.

exercise: Write a test where user B requests user A's order and expects 404, watch it fail on a naive view, then fix the view. Run manage.py check --deploy against your settings and resolve every warning, noting which ones you consciously accept.
pitfalls: @csrf_exempt on views that use cookie/session authentication.
mark_safe() or |safe on anything a user can influence.
Authenticating the user but not authorising the specific object (IDOR).
fields = "__all__" on serializers (mass assignment of is_staff, owner, status…).
DEBUG=True, hard-coded SECRET_KEY, or secrets committed to git.
Logging passwords, tokens or full request bodies.

interview.q: How does Django protect against SQL injection?
interview.a: The ORM builds queries with parameters sent separately from the SQL text, so user input is never interpreted as SQL. The risk returns with raw() / cursor.execute() when you format strings yourself; always pass parameters (%s with a list).

interview.q: How does CSRF protection work in Django?
interview.a: CsrfViewMiddleware gives each session a secret token and requires unsafe requests (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) to send it in the form or a header; a malicious site cannot read the token, so cross-site requests are rejected. It matters for cookie/session authentication; token-in-header APIs are not vulnerable the same way.

interview.q: How are XSS attacks prevented, and how can you break it?
interview.a: Django templates auto-escape variables so injected HTML/JS renders as text. You break it with mark_safe(), |safe or autoescape off on untrusted data, or by building HTML strings yourself.

interview.q: What is IDOR and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: Insecure direct object reference: an endpoint like /orders/123 returns the object to any authenticated user. Prevent it by authorising each object, e.g. get_object_or_404(Order, pk=pk, customer__user=request.user), or has_object_permission in DRF, and by testing with two users.

interview.q: CORS vs CSRF?
interview.a: CSRF is an attack where another site makes a victim's browser send an authenticated request; the defence is a token. CORS is a browser policy controlling which origins may read cross-origin responses via JavaScript; it does not stop requests from being sent. Misconfigured wildcard CORS with credentials is a vulnerability.

interview.q: How does Django store passwords?
interview.a: As a salted, iterated hash (PBKDF2 with SHA256 by default), with the algorithm and parameters stored in the value so hashers can be upgraded; plaintext passwords are never stored.

interview.q: What does manage.py check --deploy do?
interview.a: It audits settings for production risks, such as DEBUG, missing HTTPS redirect, insecure cookies, missing HSTS or a weak SECRET_KEY, and reports warnings. Running it in CI keeps risky settings from shipping.

basis: Core. CSRF, SQL injection, XSS and password hashing are in the Middle Django topic list, and SQL-injection prevention is part of the junior backend bar.
